Tomography

Words: 131 Articles: 2
Inverse problem OurBigBook.com
Tomography reconstructs an interior distribution from measurements along multiple lines or paths through it. A linear unattenuated model is the Radon transform; absorption changes it to an attenuated Radon transform.

Computed tomography

Words: 59
Tomography OurBigBook.com
Transmission measurements determine line integrals of an absorption coefficient after taking the logarithm of incident intensity divided by transmitted intensity. Under the ideal straight-ray model, these measurements are a Radon transform; filtered backprojection reconstructs a planar slice. Angular coverage, calibration and noise control matter because differentiating measured projections amplifies high frequencies. In contrast, single-photon emission computed tomography reconstructs an emitting source through a possibly attenuating medium.

Single-photon emission computed tomography

Words: 45
Tomography OurBigBook.com
A form of tomography that reconstructs an internal radioactive source from directional counts of individually emitted photons. Known spatial photon absorption gives the exponential path weight in an attenuated Radon transform. Full directed data and a suitable reconstruction formula recover the source intensity rather than a transmitted exterior-beam attenuation map.

Ill-posed inverse problem

Words: 51
Inverse problem OurBigBook.com
An inverse problem is an ill-posed problem when its specified data do not give existence, uniqueness and continuous dependence of the recovered object in the chosen spaces. Missing Fourier modes can cause nonuniqueness, while small singular values can cause instability even when a unique solution exists. Regularization of an inverse problem adds information or a stability preference to the reconstruction.

X-ray transform (Ih(γ)=∫γ​h)

Words: 491 Articles: 8
Inverse problem OurBigBook.com
The X-ray transform records integrals of a function or tensor evaluation over a specified family of curves. The curve family, parametrization and any weights are part of the definition. Straight lines, geodesics and magnetic flows give different versions; their injectivity and unavoidable potential kernels depend on that geometry.

Thermostat X-ray transform (IF​(h,θ)(γ)=∫γ​(h(γ(t))+θγ(t)​(γ˙​(t)))dt)

Words: 115 Articles: 1
X-ray transform OurBigBook.com
The transform integrates a base function and a velocity-evaluated one-form along the closed trajectories of a surface thermostat. Every exact differential form of degree one integrates to zero, because F(f∘π)=df(v). The relevant kernel theorem concerns these functions of velocity degree zero and one, rather than arbitrary functions on the unit tangent bundle.

Kernel of the thermostat X-ray transform in degrees zero and one (Fu=h∘π+θx​(v)⟹h=0, θ=df)

Words: 68
Thermostat X-ray transform OurBigBook.com
For a smooth Anosov flow generated by a surface thermostat on a closed oriented Riemannian surface, a smooth base function plus a smooth one-form is a smooth flow coboundary precisely when the base function is zero and the one-form is an exact differential form. This is the nontrivial degree-zero/one kernel theorem. It does not require negative curvature or preservation of Liouville volume. The converse follows directly from F(f∘π)=df(v). A primary proof of the kernel theorem is arxiv.org/abs/math/0601039.

Magnetic X-ray transform

Words: 112 Articles: 1
X-ray transform OurBigBook.com
The magnetic transform integrates functions or velocity-evaluated one-forms along magnetic trajectories, rather than ordinary geodesics. For closed trajectories, every exact one-form integrates to zero. Hyperbolic dynamics can make these the entire degree-one kernel.

Kernel of the magnetic X-ray transform in degrees zero and one (Fu=h(x)+ξx​(v)⟹h=0, ξ exact)

Words: 79
Magnetic X-ray transform OurBigBook.com
For a smooth Anosov magnetic flow on a closed oriented surface, a smooth function plus a smooth one-form can be a smooth flow coboundary only when the function is zero and the one-form is exact. Equivalently their sum has zero integral along every closed orbit precisely in that case, using the smooth Livsic theorem. This is the nontrivial magnetic transform kernel theorem. Exact one-forms give the converse directly, since F(w∘π)=dw(v). The theorem does not require pointwise negative Gaussian curvature.

Geodesic X-ray transform (Ig​β(γ)=∫βγ(t)​(γ˙​(t),γ˙​(t))dt)

Words: 219 Articles: 3
X-ray transform OurBigBook.com
For a symmetric covariant two-tensor, the geodesic transform integrates its evaluation on the unit velocity along boundary-to-boundary or closed geodesics, as appropriate to the manifold. A potential symmetric 2-tensor gives a total derivative along each geodesic and therefore integrates to zero on closed geodesics; boundary data require the corresponding boundary potential to vanish.

Counterexample to geodesic one-form injectivity on the round sphere (θ=x32​dx1​)

Words: 67
Geodesic X-ray transform OurBigBook.com
The displayed one-form on the unit round sphere has zero integral on every closed geodesic. Indeed, the antipodal map pulls it back to its negative, and the second half of an oriented great circle is the antipodal image of the first. Nevertheless dθ=2x3​dx3​∧dx1​ is nonzero on an open set, so the one-form is not a closed differential form and cannot be an exact differential form. Thus a curvature-free extension of one-form injectivity fails.

Pestov identity for a geodesic flow (2⟨Hφ,VXφ⟩=∥Xφ∥2+∥Hφ∥2−∫K(Vφ)2)

Words: 58
Geodesic X-ray transform OurBigBook.com
On a closed oriented Riemannian surface this integral identity follows from the canonical commutators and integration by parts against Liouville volume of a surface geodesic flow. If VXφ=−2Hφ and K<0, substitution gives ∥Xφ∥2+5∥Hφ∥2+∫(−K)(Vφ)2=0. Each term is nonnegative, forcing all three derivatives to vanish. For φ=V2u+u, the fibre equation then makes u a constant plus a fibrewise linear function, supplying the potential symmetric 2-tensor kernel.

Potential symmetric 2-tensor (β=LZ​g)

Words: 44
Geodesic X-ray transform OurBigBook.com
For a vector field Z, define β(v,w)=⟨∇v​Z,w⟩+⟨∇w​Z,v⟩. Its diagonal evaluation is 2⟨∇v​Z,v⟩. Along a geodesic this equals 2d⟨Z,γ˙​⟩/dt, so it is invisible to closed-geodesic integrals. If a fibrewise linear function u(x,v)=ηx​(v) solves Xu=β(v,v), then Z=η♯/2 gives this convention.

Forward problem

Words: 41
Inverse problem OurBigBook.com
A forward problem computes observable data f=Ku from a known state or parameter u and a specified model K. Its associated inverse problem reconstructs u from f and the model. Inverse problems can fail existence, uniqueness or continuous dependence on the data.

Residual of an inverse problem (r=Ku−f)

Words: 23
Inverse problem OurBigBook.com
The residual is the difference between predicted and observed data. Its norm measures data misfit and can determine an iteration stopping rule for regularization of an inverse problem.

Inverse scattering problem

Words: 1k Articles: 23
Inverse problem OurBigBook.com
An inverse scattering problem reconstructs a medium or obstacle from measured scattered waves. Under the Born approximation, fixed-frequency far-field data sample the Fourier transform of the scattering potential on a restricted frequency surface.

Spherical far-field range condition (∑n​(2n/(ekR))2n∑m​∣anm​∣2<∞)

Words: 138 Articles: 1
Inverse scattering problem OurBigBook.com
For an outgoing field outside a sphere of radius R, write us​=k∑n,m​in+1anm​hn(1)​(kr)Ynm​. Its far-field pattern is ∑anm​Ynm​. If its trace on that sphere lies in L2 space, Parseval's identity gives k2∑∣hn(1)​(kR)∣2∣anm​∣2<∞. The fixed-argument growth of spherical Hankel functions yields the displayed equivalent range condition, with the low-order weights defined finitely. Square summability of the far-field coefficients alone does not ensure continuation to the chosen sphere.

Unbounded spherical far-to-near-field continuation (gnm​=kin+1hn(1)​(kR)anm​)

Words: 76
Spherical far-field range condition OurBigBook.com
Continuation of a far-field pattern to a spherical trace multiplies harmonic coefficients by the displayed factor, whose magnitude grows faster than exponentially with order. A data error of size δ in one normalized high-order harmonic therefore produces near-field error δk∣hn(1)​(kR)∣, unbounded as its order increases. Some noisy square-summable far fields fail the range condition entirely. This proves unstable field continuation; bounds on actual obstacle geometry additionally require an admissible shape class and a stable boundary-extraction procedure.

Fourier diffraction theorem

Words: 89 Articles: 1
Inverse scattering problem OurBigBook.com
The Born approximation for scalar wave scattering relates an incident plane wave and the transverse Fourier transform of its scattered field to samples of the three-dimensional Fourier transform of a scattering potential on a shifted Ewald sphere. One incident direction at one frequency samples a surface, rather than an entire three-dimensional frequency region. Additional illuminations, frequencies or structural constraints are needed for a full reconstruction.

Ewald sphere (∣κ+ki​∣=k)

Words: 37
Fourier diffraction theorem OurBigBook.com
With ∣ki​∣=k, elastic scattering into a propagating wavevector ks​ samples Fourier transfer κ=ks​−ki​. These transfers satisfy the displayed shifted sphere relation. This reciprocal-space construction appears in crystallographic diffraction and the Fourier diffraction theorem.

Kirchhoff–Helmholtz representation

Words: 98 Articles: 1
Inverse scattering problem OurBigBook.com
With the normal directed out of an obstacle D into the fluid, a field solving (Δ+k2)ψ=−Q outside D has the representation
ψ(r)=∫Q(r′)Gk​(r,r′)dr′+∫∂D​[ψ∂n′​Gk​−Gk​∂n′​ψ]dS′.
(1)
Here Gk​ is the outgoing Green function for the three-dimensional Helmholtz equation and the observation point lies outside the obstacle. The formula follows from Green second identity; the normal to the exterior fluid on its inner boundary is the negative of the stated obstacle normal. The surface term represents the scattered field.

Surface representation of an obstacle far-field pattern

Words: 27
Kirchhoff–Helmholtz representation OurBigBook.com
For a scattered field satisfying ψs​=eikrf∞​(r)/r+O(r−2), the Kirchhoff–Helmholtz representation gives
f∞​(r)=−4π1​∫∂D​e−ikr⋅r′[∂n′​ψs​+ik(r⋅n′)ψs​]dS′.
(2)
The sign assumes the normal points out of the obstacle.

Herglotz wave function

Words: 148 Articles: 2
Inverse scattering problem OurBigBook.com
A Herglotz wave function is a superposition of incident plane waves,
vg​(r)=∫S2​eikd⋅rg(d)dS(d),g∈L2(S2).
(3)
It solves the Helmholtz equation everywhere and is real analytic. The finite sphere area makes the density integrable, so each spatial derivative can be taken under the integral.

Herglotz pairing with an obstacle far field

Words: 106 Articles: 1
Herglotz wave function OurBigBook.com
Pairing a far-field pattern with the conjugate density of a Herglotz wave function converts the angular integral into boundary data:
∫S2​f∞​(r)g(r)​dS=4π1​∫∂D​[ψs​∂n​vg​​−vg​​∂n​ψs​]dS.
(4)
This follows by substituting the surface representation of an obstacle far-field pattern and interchanging the integrals.
Shape recovery from a Herglotz boundary identity
Words: 78
Herglotz pairing with an obstacle far field OurBigBook.com
If measured far-field patterns determine a density g and its Herglotz wave function equals a prescribed spherical wave on the obstacle boundary, that trace identity can locate the boundary. A star-shaped axisymmetric obstacle can be represented by one radial function h(θ). Numerically, expand g and h in suitable bases, match the far-field constraints, and minimize the complex boundary residual at angular collocation points, using regularization of an inverse problem for noise and small singular values. A single scalar pairing constraint alone does not determine an arbitrary density.

Scattering potential (V)

Words: 177 Articles: 3
Inverse scattering problem OurBigBook.com
For a refractive index n(r) and background wavenumber k0​, one sign convention defines the scattering potential by V=k02​(1−n2). The total field then satisfies (Δ+k02​)ψ=Vψ.
The opposite convention V=k02​(n2−1) gives (Δ+k02​)ψ=−Vψ and reverses the sign attached to the corresponding Green-function integral. Either convention is valid when used consistently.

Born approximation for scalar wave scattering

Words: 126 Articles: 2
Scattering potential OurBigBook.com
Using V=k02​(n2−1), the scalar Lippmann-Schwinger equation is ψ=ψi​+∫D​Gk0​​Vψ. The Born approximation replaces the total field inside the integral by the known incident field:
ψB​=ψi​+∫D​Gk0​​(r,r′)V(r′)ψi​(r′)dr′.
(5)
For a unit plane wave, its far-field pattern is (4π)−1∫D​V(r′)eik0​(r0​−r)⋅r′dr′. Thus each incident direction samples a shifted sphere in the Fourier transform of the potential.
Born non-scattering contrasts at one incident direction (V=[Δ2+4(ki​⋅∇)2]h)
Words: 45
Born approximation for scalar wave scattering OurBigBook.com
For real h∈Cc∞​(D), the displayed real compactly supported contrast has Fourier transform V(κ)=[∣κ∣4−4(ki​⋅κ)2]h(κ). This vanishes on the shifted Ewald sphere because ∣κ∣2+2ki​⋅κ=0 there. Thus nonzero contrasts can have zero fixed-frequency, fixed-incidence Born approximation data. A small amplitude preserves weak contrast and a positive refractive index.
Born series (ψs​=∑j≥1​Tjψi​)
Words: 27
Born approximation for scalar wave scattering OurBigBook.com
The Born series is the Neumann series expansion of the Lippmann-Schwinger equation. Its terms describe successive orders of wave scattering; convergence is ensured, for example, by a scattering operator norm smaller than one.

Rytov approximation

Words: 395 Articles: 6
Inverse scattering problem OurBigBook.com
The Rytov approximation writes a total wave field as ψ=ψi​eϕ and linearizes the equation for the complex logarithmic perturbation ϕ. At first order, ψi​ϕ equals the first Born approximation scattered field, so
ψR​=ψi​exp(ψs,B​/ψi​).
(6)
It can remain useful when phase accumulation is appreciable but local scattering is weak.

First-Rytov coherent mean (E[ψR​]=ψi​exp(μ2E[χ12​]/2))

Words: 53
Rytov approximation OurBigBook.com
If the first logarithmic perturbation χ1​ is a centered linear functional of a Gaussian random field, the complex Gaussian exponential moment gives the displayed mean of the first Rytov approximation ψR​=ψi​eμχ1​. This is the mean of the truncated logarithmic model. A nonzero mean of the omitted second logarithmic perturbation can change the true field mean at order μ2.

Phase covariance in the first Rytov approximation (Cov(φ1​,φ2​)=∬b1​b2​CW​)

Words: 56
Rytov approximation OurBigBook.com
For a centered real scattering potential fluctuation W and the imaginary part b of the incident-field-weighted Green function, φ(r)=−∫b(r,r′)W(r′)dr′. Its mean vanishes, and its covariance function is the double integral of the two deterministic kernels against the covariance function of W. The correlation of the refractive index itself is insufficient when the scattering potential depends quadratically on that index.

Validity of the first Rytov approximation

Words: 53
Rytov approximation OurBigBook.com
The Rytov approximation omits the quadratic gradient source in the logarithmic wave perturbation equation. Its next correction solves Li​χ2​=−∇χ1​⋅∇χ1​. Control of the propagated correction, weak amplitude fluctuations and avoidance of field zeros are needed. An appreciable smooth accumulated phase can be retained by exponentiation; small total phase is not the same condition as small local phase gradients.

Logarithmic wave perturbation (χ=log(ψ/ψi​))

Words: 42
Rytov approximation OurBigBook.com
The logarithmic wave perturbation measures relative complex amplitude and phase through ψ=ψi​eχ. A continuous branch requires nonzero incident and total fields in the region considered. For the Helmholtz equation with scattering potential convention L0​ψ=−Vψ, its equation is (Δ+2∇logψi​⋅∇)χ+∇χ⋅∇χ=−V. The dot product is bilinear, not a squared modulus.

Gaussian intensity in the first Rytov approximation

Words: 144 Articles: 1
Rytov approximation OurBigBook.com
Let ψR​=ψi​eϕ1​ with unit-modulus incidence and ϕ1​=∫D​K(r,r′)V(r′)dr′. For a centered real Gaussian random field V, the exponential moment of a Gaussian linear functional gives
E∣ψR​∣2=exp[21​∫D​∫D​a(r′)a(r′′)CV​(r′−r′′)dr′dr′′],a=2ReK.
(7)
Here CV​ is the autocorrelation function of a random field. Both the covariance E∣ϕ1​∣2 and the generally nonzero term ReEϕ12​ enter the exponent; dropping the latter is not justified for an arbitrary finite real random medium.

For a scalar BV space function, clipping to [−M,M] partitions its coarea formula for BV functions into middle and tail levels. This is stronger than the triangle inequality and is specific to scalar monotone clipping. It supports residual-preserving clipping of an ROF minimizer.

Zero Bregman distance and supporting faces
Words: 69
Bregman divergence OurBigBook.com
For p∈∂J(v), zero Bregman distance means that J(u) equals the supporting affine function J(v)+⟨p,u−v⟩. If J is strictly convex, two distinct contact points are impossible: convexity along their segment would be strict, while the subgradient inequality supplies the opposite bound. Thus zero distance then implies u=v. Without strict convexity, J(s)=∣s∣, v=1, p=1 gives zero distance for every u≥0. These are all on the same supporting face.

Landweber iteration OurBigBook.com
For nonzero compact operator A, step 0<τ<2/∥A∥2, and data admitting a minimum-norm least-squares solution x†, zero-initialized Landweber iteration satisfies
∥xn​−x†∥2=∑i​∣1−τσi2​∣2nσi2​∣⟨y,ui​⟩∣2​⟶0.

The Picard criterion makes the majorant summable, so the dominated convergence theorem proves this limit. No mesh-independent or singular-value-independent strict contraction factor is required. Without solvable projected data, the iterates need not have a limit in the solution Hilbert space, even when their residuals approach the least-squares infimum.

Landweber iteration OurBigBook.com
The Landweber spectral filter progressively admits smaller singular-value components. Its approximation bias tends to zero on exact admissible data, but its noise amplification grows. With ∥A∥≤1, a sufficient a priori regularization parameter choice is n(δ)→∞ and n(δ)​δ→0. Taking regularization parameter α=1/n expresses this as α→0 and δ/α​→0; the noise-bias decomposition for linear regularization proves convergence.

Moore–Penrose inverse of an operator (A†)

Words: 111 Articles: 1
Normal equation for a linear inverse problem OurBigBook.com
For a bounded operator A:X→Y between Hilbert spaces, the Moore–Penrose inverse maps admissible data to the unique minimum-norm least-squares solution. If (σj​,uj​,vj​) is a singular system of a compact operator, then
A†y=∑j​σj​⟨y,uj​⟩​vj​
(37)
on the data for which this series converges.
More precisely, its domain is ranA⊕(ranA)⊥. It vanishes on (ranA)⊥ and takes values in (kerA)⊥. An infinite-rank compact operator on infinite-dimensional spaces has singular values approaching zero, so its inverse on its range is generally unbounded; Picard criterion specifies admissible data.

Words: 32

A minimum-norm least-squares solution minimizes ∥Ax−y∥ and, among all such minimizers, minimizes ∥x∥. It lies in (kerA)⊥ and equals A†y when the Moore–Penrose inverse of an operator is defined at y.
